title: The Impact of Trade on Economic Prosperity

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
- Method: Instrumental Variables (2SLS) using geographic distance (z) as an instrument for trade volume (x).
- Why: Trade volume is endogenous in the GDP per capita equation due to reverse causality and omitted variables (e.g., institutions). Distance shifts trade costs and thus trade volume but is plausibly unrelated to unobserved determinants of income, conditional on controls.
- Key assumptions:
  - Relevance: Cov(z, x | controls) ≠ 0 (first-stage F-stat sufficiently large).
  - Exclusion: z affects y only through x, conditional on controls (no direct effect of distance on income beyond what is captured by controls).
  - Independence: z is as good as randomly assigned with respect to unobservables in the outcome equation, conditional on controls.
  - Linearity and correct specification of controls in the structural model.
  - Interpretation: With a binary instrument, the 2SLS estimate is a LATE for “compliers.”

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load packages
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(AER)
  library(sandwich)
  library(lmtest)
})

# 1) Read data
df <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s78_data.csv")

# Quick sanity checks
stopifnot(all(c("y","x","z","controls") %in% names(df)))
df$z <- as.numeric(df$z) # ensure numeric/binary

# 2) OLS (naive benchmark)
m_ols <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)
ols_coef <- coef(summary(m_ols))["x", "Estimate"]
ols_se   <- coef(summary(m_ols))["x", "Std. Error"]

# 3) First stage: x on z and controls
m_fs <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = df)
fs_sum <- summary(m_fs)
fs_bz  <- coef(fs_sum)["z", "Estimate"]
fs_tz  <- coef(fs_sum)["z", "t value"]
fs_F   <- as.numeric(fs_tz^2)  # with 1 instrument, t^2 equals partial F

# 4) 2SLS: y on x and controls, instrument x with z
m_iv <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | controls + z, data = df)
# Heteroskedasticity-robust SEs
vc_iv  <- vcovHC(m_iv, type = "HC1")
ct_iv  <- coeftest(m_iv, vcov. = vc_iv)
iv_bx  <- ct_iv["x", "Estimate"]
iv_se  <- ct_iv["x", "Std. Error"]
iv_ci  <- c(iv_bx - 1.96*iv_se, iv_bx + 1.96*iv_se)

# Diagnostics: weak instrument F and Wu-Hausman (if available)
iv_diag <- tryCatch(summary(m_iv, diagnostics = TRUE)$diagnostics, error = function(e) NULL)
weakF <- weakP <- wuStat <- wuP <- NA
if (!is.null(iv_diag)) {
  wr <- grep("Weak", rownames(iv_diag))
  if (length(wr) > 0) {
    weakF <- as.numeric(iv_diag[wr[1], "statistic"])
    weakP <- as.numeric(iv_diag[wr[1], "p-value"])
  }
  hr <- grep("Wu", rownames(iv_diag))
  if (length(hr) > 0) {
    wuStat <- as.numeric(iv_diag[hr[1], "statistic"])
    wuP    <- as.numeric(iv_diag[hr[1], "p-value"])
  }
}

# 5) Reduced-form: y on z and controls
m_rf <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = df)
rf_bz <- coef(summary(m_rf))["z", "Estimate"]
rf_se <- coef(summary(m_rf))["z", "Std. Error"]

# 6) Robustness A: add nonlinearity in controls
df$controls2 <- df$controls^2
m_iv_poly <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls + controls2 | controls + controls2 + z, data = df)
vc_iv_poly <- vcovHC(m_iv_poly, type = "HC1")
ct_iv_poly <- coeftest(m_iv_poly, vcov. = vc_iv_poly)
iv_bx_poly <- ct_iv_poly["x", "Estimate"]
iv_se_poly <- ct_iv_poly["x", "Std. Error"]
iv_ci_poly <- c(iv_bx_poly - 1.96*iv_se_poly, iv_bx_poly + 1.96*iv_se_poly)

# 7) Robustness B: trim extreme x (1% tails)
qlo <- quantile(df$x, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE)
qhi <- quantile(df$x, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)
df_trim <- subset(df, x >= qlo & x <= qhi)
m_iv_trim <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | controls + z, data = df_trim)
vc_iv_trim <- vcovHC(m_iv_trim, type = "HC1")
ct_iv_trim <- coeftest(m_iv_trim, vcov. = vc_iv_trim)
iv_bx_trim <- ct_iv_trim["x", "Estimate"]
iv_se_trim <- ct_iv_trim["x", "Std. Error"]
iv_ci_trim <- c(iv_bx_trim - 1.96*iv_se_trim, iv_bx_trim + 1.96*iv_se_trim)

# 8) Print clear numerical results
cat("Naive OLS:\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x (OLS) = %.4f  (SE = %.4f)\n\n", ols_coef, ols_se))

cat("First Stage:\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_{z->x} = %.4f,  t = %.3f,  partial F = %.3f\n\n", fs_bz, fs_tz, fs_F))

cat("IV (2SLS) Main Estimate with robust SEs:\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x (IV) = %.4f  (robust SE = %.4f),  95%% CI = [%.4f, %.4f]\n",
            iv_bx, iv_se, iv_ci[1], iv_ci[2]))
if (!is.na(weakF)) {
  cat(sprintf("  Weak-instrument first-stage F = %.3f (p = %.3f)\n", weakF, weakP))
}
if (!is.na(wuStat)) {
  cat(sprintf("  Wu-Hausman endogeneity test: stat = %.3f (p = %.3f)\n", wuStat, wuP))
}
cat("\n")

cat("Reduced Form (y on z):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_{z->y} = %.4f  (SE = %.4f)\n\n", rf_bz, rf_se))

cat("Robustness A (add controls^2):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x (IV, poly controls) = %.4f  (robust SE = %.4f),  95%% CI = [%.4f, %.4f]\n\n",
            iv_bx_poly, iv_se_poly, iv_ci_poly[1], iv_ci_poly[2]))

cat("Robustness B (trim 1%% tails of x):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x (IV, trimmed) = %.4f  (robust SE = %.4f),  95%% CI = [%.4f, %.4f]\n",
            iv_bx_trim, iv_se_trim, iv_ci_trim[1], iv_ci_trim[2]))
```

## 3. Expected Findings
- Sign: Positive. Higher trade volume should increase economic prosperity via specialization, larger markets, and technology diffusion.
- Magnitude: With standardized-like variables in the preview, an IV coefficient in the range 0.3–0.7 (elasticity-like effect on log GDP per capita per 1 SD increase in trade volume) is plausible. IV may differ from OLS depending on the direction of endogeneity; if richer countries trade more (reverse causality), OLS may be upward-biased; if unobserved institutions raise both income and trade, OLS may also be upward-biased. The IV estimate isolates variation from distance-driven trade costs.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use geographic distance as an instrument for trade volume to isolate its impact on GDP per capita.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Increased trade volume has a significant negative effect on log GDP per capita.
